decision.audit_notes: Verified current-session dialogue; decision evidence remapped to cleaned source.

evidence.text: Oh 17? Gosh. I'm just — I’m gobstopped. I think you're bright and I give your father so much credit for supporting your vision and seeing the merit of it. And I do think it has tremendous merit. It's a little early for me to go in, right now. Because I think there are some challenges up ahead. And I'd like to see how the company addresses those challenges. So I'm going to pass, but I'd like to say on the record that choose a school. Because this is not going to be, if you thought this up at 17 years old —

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: And last year when I got my license, I asked my dad if I could get a car. And he said sure, but only if I could find out a way to pay for it. So I came up with a plan to lease out a car for the summer, and drive people back and forth from LA to Vegas on the weekends to make up for the lease and insurance payments.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So that was then, and here we are now. Tesloop is building the world's leading sustainable mobility service. We're perfecting inter-city transit between 50 and 300 miles. So we're here today raising $1 million to do this, $500,000 of which we've already closed. So to clarify, we're here today to raise $500,000 more.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Very well done. Are you a senior? You must be a senior.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yeah, I'm a senior this year.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So you were able to lease a Tesla because you're 18 years old?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: When I originally leased it, I was 16, so I leased it under my... Well, that's kind of complicated, but my dad had it leased for me through a third-party service.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Because I can imagine a 16-year-old going and saying, hello, I'd like to lease it for three months, and if you don't like it, happiness. Um so, where are you going to school, do you know?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Where do you want to go to school?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: All my apps are due at the end of the month.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I know. So what's your first choice?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Well, see there's two paths I'm either going to take. I'm either going to go out of state, but that really creates a problem with me working with Tesloop, still.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Or I can stay in the area and still work with Tesloop. So I'm really undecided where I'm going to go to college. I'm applying to a lot of different universities, and...

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Are you worried that school is going to get in the way of running this company?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: I think there's going to be a point where I'm going to have to pick one to put all my time and effort into. And the way I'm seeing it, it's school.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: If that happens, who runs the company?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Well, there's five other people working full time right now. So...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How old are they? They're not in school?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: No, they're not in school. They're very seasoned entrepreneurs.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: He was going to say very old, they're very old.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Are they as old as we are?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: They're in their mid-20s.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Between mid-20s to 50s.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That old?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: And everyone's working full time.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: And what's your role at the company today?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Right now I'm doing, well since school started, over the summer I work full time. And then I just kind of do side-tasks when I'm still working in school. Like today, I still had to go to school.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: How did you bring in your CEO? Where'd you find him and make that connection?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: The CEO is my dad.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's great.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So I've known him for a little bit.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So I'm trying to figure out, and maybe I've completely lost this, exactly what this business is. Is it fleets? Can you explain exactly what it is? Is it just me?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: No, I'm having the same, I don't understand it.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: No, it's a good question. So we're kind of like South-West on the ground. Where we drive people from one city to another in Teslas —

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh!

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: — between their pick-up points, for a pretty low economically-priced ticket.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So it's an Uber for Teslas?

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: There’s a driver.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: For long distance — long distance trips. Between how many miles?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: 50 to 300 is our targeted distance. That's what we call the electric haul, where the economics of electric cars really benefit you. Because further than that you have to charge the car too much. Shorter than that, a gas-powered car kind of benefits you because you don't have to charge.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So how does that work? You get free charging?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yeah. We get free unlimited charging at the Supercharge booths.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But everyone does, not just you?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Everyone does.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So I brought the idea up with Elon Musk at the shareholders meeting in 2015, and at that point he assured me that Tesla would pay for all of the fuel costs for long distance travel in the Model S forever.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Do you mind me asking you how you got to Elon?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Just at the shareholders meeting.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So your father must be on the board? Or somebody?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: No. I just bought a couple of Tesla stocks in 2014, and so did he, so we were both able to get into the meeting. So then —

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That’s so great.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: — you can just stand in line pretty much and ask questions. And I asked him a question which resulted in him telling us, or telling everyone basically, that Tesla was going to supply free long-distance travel forever on their Supercharger network.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I suppose there could be, they might draw a line between consumer usage and business usage?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: As of right now they haven't drawn that line. We are in somewhat collaborating with Tesla. They're aware of what's happening. They're aware we're using it for commercial use. And right now, they haven't said anything about that. And there are a lot of people that work in the Tesla stores as well as executives that are aware that we exist. And they haven't had any issues yet.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I mean, it's a good idea. What's to say that Uber or any other ride-sharing would not just lift this? Or Lyft?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Well, we think there are a couple of reasons why Uber can't do this. The first is that, for the next four years this can only be done on Teslas. They have the only platform with the big batteries and super charging and nice cars that allows this model to happen. And for strategic reasons, Uber can't really work with Tesla, because then Tesla would have all the information to their sensory data and Uber would have none of that. So they'd be kind of losing all the information about their cars.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Are you leasing the cars?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yes. Well, we have a leasing company that leases the cars for us, and then offers us a zero down. It's around $2500 to $3000 a month for the cars.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How many cars?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Right now we have one Model S and two Model Xs.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And what cities are you servicing now?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: We launched between LA and Vegas, well LA and Orange County to Vegas and back.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: How are the routes booked? Does the driver wait in Palm Springs for a few hours if the timings don't match? And then you're paying the driver to wait? Just walk me through that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That’s a good question.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So right now we have two cars running in Palm Springs, and they leave at 8 am and 1 pm from Palm Springs. And then there's returns at 11am and 3pm.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So set times? Okay.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Those aren't specifically set times. How we've kind of been doing it right now where is if the first person to book wants it within an hour difference, we can accommodate that. And then the other people booking will just have to go with the first person's time.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: What's the cost?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So, that's pretty dynamic on the day and the demand. But for Vegas, it varies between $59 to $129 one way per person.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: But I can book in advance?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: You can book two months in advance.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Two months in advance.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And what's the Palm Springs cost?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: And Palm Springs is $39 to $59.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How long does that trip take?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: The trip's about two and a half to 2:45 to three, depending on traffic.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And somebody could pay $39 for that?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I can't even get from San Francisco to Atherton for $39.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: San Francisco to Atherton? I can't get from the Ferry Building to the Mission some days.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Is that right? I can pay $39 and go for a two-and-a-half-hour drive to get to Palm Springs?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yep. It is a shared car, so there will be a possibility... We have in the Model X, four available seats to book. In the Model S, three.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Okay. But even if you don't fill up the cars, I still pay $39?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yeah, you still pay the same.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How did you price this? Just curiosity. Because it seems quite low, and it seems that you could probably price this a wee bit higher.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: We're pricing it basically to meet all of our expenses. We're not, as of right now, because the expenses are going to be trending towards zero in the future, this cost for right now is going to remain the same. And maybe two years from now, that's when we get really...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Create revenue.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Why would you only price this to cover your costs? When I think the market would bear you charging at least $50 on the low side, and $75 on the high side. I'm just trying to figure out...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What's the competition? How can you get from LA to Palm Springs, or LA to Vegas now?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Plane. Bus.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What are the competitors and what's the cost?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: So for Palm Springs, the only real other travel alternatives would be fly there, which is expensive. It's almost $200 or $250. You can take an Amtrak, but that's not a direct route.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How about a bus?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: The buses aren't, we wouldn't call them competitors, because it's a completely different experience.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But actually you're supporting, Phil, my question and it's that it seems like you're the only horse in town. So why not price yourself a bit higher no matter what? So that you're actually not just covering your costs. All we are saying is that, we think you're onto something.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's the good news.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I think you're leaving money on the table.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: We think you're leaving money on the table. That's the even better news.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How much revenue did you do last month?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Last month we did in total around 27 thousand.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: With three cars?

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: With three cars.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So you raised $500,000 of a million. How did you raise that? And what was the valuation? I missed that. You were raising $1 million.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: It's $1 million and a $6 million cap.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Six cap, okay.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I have a question, too. We've all sort of danced around, we brought it up a little bit, but you built a company that is, you built it entirely on the Tesla platform. And Tesla is not really a platform company. They didn't build a platform for other people to build businesses on. I mean, you did it in the name, Tesloop. And I think that if you got really big either Tesla is going to buy you or they're going to shut you down on that name because it's definitely a trademark infringement. I think that's a problem. And then you've built your cost structure on using Tesla cars and free-charging, which Musk said would remain free. But that doesn't mean free for commercial use. And you don't have a contract with him. I would feel great if you had had a personal conversation with Tesla. Something to say, we acknowledge that your business exists and we give you freedom to operate. I think if you get big, Tesla is either going to have to buy you or they're going to have to shut you down.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Or they're going to build this themselves.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: And then shut you down.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: We don't think Tesla is going to try and do this themselves. Elon Musk is not about creating city to city transit. Right now, one of his biggest focuses is on automating manufacturing. And there's a lot of focus on that from Tesla and the rest of his companies. We don't think Tesla directly will come into our exact model. And I would also differ to say that Tesla did create a platform to be built upon. They have open-sourced a lot of their data. They're very accepting of use of their Supercharging from us. And they have a lot of future implications that are going to arise from their platform.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I think this is awesome — this company you've built. It's really great. So don't take this to be brutal criticism. But they're accepting of a three-car company using Superchargers. It's very expensive for Tesla to build out these networks. And if you scale up and you've got 100 cars on the road to Palm Springs every day, and the other Tesla drivers who are not commercial drivers cannot get a Supercharger, I guarantee you Tesla is going to say, "No commercial use, you are not allowed to use our stations." Because they built this network for their private owners.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right. They didn't build this for commercial use.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yeah. It comes down to if we're at the scale where Tesla won't let us operate on this, we're going to have to pay for electricity. And that will all come into play in the future. But for the foreseeable future, there's no issues with Tesla and the Supercharging.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So I commend you for being so young and having so much vision. In fact, I'm dumbfounded.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I'm going to kill my kids for not. I'm going to say, there's this kid, he sat there, he's 18 years old, and he came up with this business.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: 17 right now.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh 17? Gosh. I'm just — I’m gobstopped. I think you're bright and I give your father so much credit for supporting your vision and seeing the merit of it. And I do think it has tremendous merit. It's a little early for me to go in, right now. Because I think there are some challenges up ahead. And I'd like to see how the company addresses those challenges. So I'm going to pass, but I'd like to say on the record that choose a school. Because this is not going to be, if you thought this up at 17 years old —

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Well, to clarify, it would be community college in LA versus school out of state.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I'm saying as a mother, I'm saying to you, this company will run itself with your father and everyone else. You don't need to be a part of it right this second. I would put your education first and try to get into the best school possible because if you're doing this and you have this vision at 17 years old, you are going to have a lot of other ones. And I would love for you to have the education to know how to build a business because I think you have many more in you. This is personal advice. Prioritize your education. Go to the best school. And you can always say that "I started a company when I was 16 years old." That's all I'm saying as a mother.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: I'll take that to heart.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Please do.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I want to —

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Just to contradict Jillian a little bit, I have my older son who while in college took a leave of absence to start a company. Because he couldn't do both at the same time. And he started a company called Klink, which is alcohol delivery, and he's crushing it. He's doing great. And he'll eventually go back to school. But he's on leave of absence now.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So he took a gap year?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Gap years. But in any case…

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Gap years.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: There's no right or wrong.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And I want to say that...

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Criticizing parenting styles — that never goes down a happy road.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I want to say also that I'm a Tesla evangelist. I've been a Tesla owner for four years. I've had two of them. Love the cars. Love the company. And I think what you're doing is really cool. I think you have a lot of challenges ahead of you. I think there's perhaps more competitive pressures coming in the near future than you're accounting for. There are a lot of other less expensive electric cars that are going to be introduced in the next year or two that will have the same seating capacity. So I'm just not Supercharged up about the deal. Did you catch that? I got him to laugh. I got him to laugh.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: He's good.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: He noticed my pun.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: He got the pun.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So I'll do what I can to help you, and I wish you all the best. And again, I think you're a rock star but I'm going to pass.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: The initiative you're taking is incredible. You're incredibly inspiring. I think that you have an entrepreneurial — I mean it's clear you have an entrepreneurial mind. You speak like an entrepreneur. You use all the right terminology. You're thinking about things in a very scrappy and creative way, which is awesome. So keep doing that. But this feels like a really cool hack. And you have some revenue. But I would just need to see a little bit more of that before I would go in. So right now it's a pass, but keep up the good work.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: All right, thank you.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: So, to Howie's hack point, I think a lot of great businesses have been built on the back of hacks. Sort of taking advantage of loopholes in the system. Your first car was a loophole in the system, basically.

turns.speaker: Haydn
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: So I've got no problem with that whatsoever. My problem is that I think you haven't thought through yet, or you're not at the stage yet, of figuring out how to move from the hack to the sustainable company. There are a ton, a ton of operational issues that you haven't had to address yet. And I think you're super sharp, you've got this great team. I think you can address these issues, but we haven't seen that yet. I don't even think you know yet what you don't know. And you won't know that until you've got 20 or 30 cars on the road. And so you're definitely a little bit early for me, because of those reasons. Without really raising the ire of Tesla you can build a $100,000 a month business. A nice business. I just think to get to that real next level, the $10 million, $50 million, $100 million, billion dollar business, it's a really different business from what you have now. So for me, it's a pass.
